files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close checklist

Prepared by A. Whitcomb. Complete these in sequence and initial the workpapers as you go.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July. If such a period exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that in some months every payroll run pays in-month.
3. Confirm that June prepaid amortization agrees with the prepaid schedule and supporting contracts. Check the GL first so nothing is recorded twice. If the June entry is missing, book all June prepaid amortization in ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month an item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after first verifying the amount already recorded in the GL.
5. Compare the June vendor-bill documents with the GL expense coding. Reclass anything miscoded to the correct expense account.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after all entries and reclassifications from items 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Beacon Ledger Software began when a former implementation consultant and a product-minded engineer kept hearing the same complaint from growing service businesses: month-end work was scattered across spreadsheets, inboxes, and accounting systems that did not communicate cleanly. They started by building a practical close workspace for a handful of finance teams, then shaped the product around the routines controllers actually perform.

The company sells cloud software that organizes reconciliations, supporting documents, close checklists, review notes, and recurring accounting workflows. Its customers are typically small and midsize businesses that need more control and visibility without the overhead of a large enterprise platform.

The team has a distinctly hands-on flavor. Product staff sit in on customer calls, engineers are known to ask unusually specific questions about journal-entry support, and the customer team keeps a running list of workflow annoyances worth fixing. Sales is consultative rather than flashy, while marketing leans on practical education for finance operators.

The current focus is steady execution: serving existing customers well, improving integrations, tightening internal processes, and making the product easier to adopt. Beacon Ledger Software remains an ordinary going concern, balancing product development with the everyday discipline of running a growing SaaS business.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Positioning
Make Beacon Ledger Software the practical close-management choice for lean finance teams. Keep the message grounded in cleaner handoffs, visible ownership, and fewer spreadsheet-driven surprises.

## Q3 priorities
- Refresh the core website narrative and customer proof points.
- Publish a close-readiness guide built around real controller workflows.
- Run recurring educational webinars with product and customer-success participation.
- Recruit a small group of accounting advisers for a partner co-marketing pilot.

## Q4 priorities
- Turn webinar questions into short articles, checklists, and product demonstrations.
- Develop customer stories focused on adoption and day-to-day usability.
- Expand the strongest partner pilot into repeatable joint content.
- Refresh nurture emails for evaluators who are not yet ready for a sales conversation.

## Operating approach
Favor useful, specific material over broad brand claims. Marketing and sales should review lead quality together, while customer success supplies recurring themes from onboarding and support conversations. Final campaign scope remains subject to planning after the Q2 close.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from your predecessor

A. Whitcomb — a few things that will save you some hunting during the close:

- The bank's own service fees and charges usually show up near the end of the statement. We have historically picked those up and booked them at close.
- Do not assume the June vendor-bill expense coding is right. A couple of bills may have been routed to the wrong accounts; use the documents in `bills/` as the authoritative support and reclass as needed.
- The budget was fixed early, at the start of Q2. The one-off June items were never planned, so they should explain most of the larger budget-to-actual variances.
- Payroll timing matters this month: the June 16-30 payroll run does not pay until the first days of July. The payroll register has the detail.
